 Learn more National Bank Holdings has delivered a 27.1% share price gain over the past 3 years, which naturally raises a question for anyone looking at the stock today. Is the current valuation still grounded in the returns the bank earns on the capital it deploys into its lending and fee businesses, or is the price now running ahead of those economics? 
 A 27.1% move over 3 years puts real weight on whether National Bank Holdings is converting its capital base into returns that can support that kind of compounding. 
 The bank's earnings power depends on how efficiently it turns its deposit base and equity into interest income and fee revenue, which can influence both reinvestment capacity and shareholder distributions over time. 
 What if you looked at National Bank Holdings through its earnings instead? See why National Bank Holdings's 30.3x P/E tells a different valuation story . 
 The issue now is whether the returns National Bank Holdings earns on its capital are strong and durable enough to justify the price investors are being asked to pay today. 
 If you are weighing whether National Bank Holdings' 27.1% three year return is backed by the returns it earns on its capital, it can help to compare that lens against 31 resilient stocks with low risk scores . 
 Does National Bank Holdings Look Undervalued on Excess Returns? 
 The Excess Returns approach looks at how effectively National Bank Holdings turns each dollar of equity into earnings above its equity cost. In this case, the firm's stable EPS input of $3.60 per share is compared with a cost of equity of $2.90 per share, resulting in an estimated excess return of $0.70 for every share of capital deployed. 
 That spread is supported by an average return on equity of 8.99%, which the model uses to anchor a stable book value estimate of $40.06 per share, compared with a current book value of $36.71 per share. You are paying a share price of $36.91 for that equity base, while the Excess Returns projections put National Bank Holdings' estimated intrinsic value substantially above the current share price.
